newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK CROWN NEARS PARITY ON FOREIGN MONEY RETREAT.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK CROWN NEARS PARITY ON FOREIGN MONEY RETREAT.

text.p: The Slovak crown eased to near its currency basket parity on Thursday, after a sharp fall in money market rates and a weaker crown fix by the central bank prompted foreign players to pull out, dealers said.
"The crown is quiet low now, but the question is whether it will attract some foreign inflows back with deposit rates declining," Tibor Fratrik, a foreign exchange dealer at ING Baring, told Reuters.
Dealers were mixed about the chances falling crown deposit rates could attract foreigners to place funds again.

"The crown may fall to below its parity again, but then it can trigger foreign players to deposit for one to three months -- terms which are declining at a slower pace -- and then rebound again," Emil Vitazka of VUB Bank said.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) continued to fix the crown weaker against the market trend on Thursday, putting it 0.55 percent above its 60/40 mark/dollar basket parity, after fixing it at +0.70 percent on Wednesday.

Prompted by the fix, the market pushed the crown lower by late afternoon trading to 32.849 against the dollar and 19.499 against the mark, or 0.06 percent above parity, after opening at about +0.85 percent.

Earlier on Thursday, the NBS said it had cut the average rate in its morning's tender for seven-day reverse repurchase to 14.95 percent, after 16.75 percent in the previous reverse repo tender with a similar maturity, giving the market another downward signal.

The move drew down the country's interbank money market rates an average of 100 basis points to a bid range of 16.7-17.5 percent on all terms while one-day funds hit a low of 1.0 percent as the market squared up for Saturday's minimum reserve deadline.

Dealers said that the bulk of the estimated $380 million which had flowed into the country since the beginning of the year when the central bank further tightened, boosting rates to record highs of 26 percent, had left the country.

"The interest rate differential players who had boosted trading volumes have left, but the spot traders who do not care about deposit rates have arrived now, and I think we will not fall below parity," Peter Koprna, a Slovenska Sporitelna dealer, said.
